summary: Counsel on record for the Appellant(s) : Mr. Pradep Misra Mr. Manoj Kumar Sharma for App. 1 1. The present Appeal has been filed by Delhi Transco Limited **,** challenging the order dated 31.08.2017 in Petition No. 18/2017 **(“Impugned Order”** ) passed 8. Heard Mr. Pradeep Mishra, learned counsel on behalf of the Appellant, Mr Dhananjay Baijal, learned counsel on behalf of the State Commission, and Mr. Rahul Kinra, learned counsel for the Respondent No 2 to 4, perused the Impugned Order dated 31.08.2017, written submission filed by the parties. The Appellant, is aggrieved by incorrect computations in the Impugned Order on following issues: Our consideration and views on each of these issues are deliberated in following paragraphs: 11. It is also affirmed on behalf of State Commission that it has already been submitted in its reply that “ _Appellant has submitted the A&G expenses as Rs 22.19 Crore against A&G expenses of Rs 21.54 Crore as indicated in financial statement for FY 2011-12. It is submitted that it is open to the Commission to reconsider this issue on the basis of audited financial statements in subsequent tariff orders and therefore this issue requires no interference by this Tribunal at_ . _this stage”_ 16. We therefore find no infirmity in the reasoning adopted by the State Commission. The disallowance of the additional water charges (arrears) is in consonance with the applicable regulatory framework and the settled principles governing controllable costs. Accordingly, the issue is decided against the Appellant, and the Impugned Order is upheld to the extent of disallowance of the arrears of water charges as claimed. “ _It is humbly submitted that the impact of change in working capital of previous year is seemingly not reflected in the subsequent year computation of RRB closing. It is submitted that the same will be considered by the Commission in its subsequent tariff order and does not require the interference of the Hon'ble Tribunal at this stage_ ” 32. We find merit in the submissions of State Commissions and considering that the open access consumer remains in the system and for FY 2017-18, there is possibility of earning this income and moreover in the true-up of FY 2017-18, only the actual non- tariff income shall be considered, thereby protecting the interest of Appellant. It has also been informed, that State Commission in its order dated 31.07.2019, has considered Rs 574.33 Crore in the True up of FY 2017-18 on account of Non –Tariff Income, however same is under challenge before this Tribunal in Appeal 59 of 2021, which is pending adjudication. Accordingly, in our considered view, at this stage when True up exercise for FY 2017-18 has already been completed by State Commission, Impugned Order needs no interference on this issue. 4 _5.1 The contention of the Petitioner/Appellant is that the Appellant has claimed Rs. 201.14 crore as against Rs. 23.51 crore computed by the Commission as there is a significant difference in the amount claimed by the Appellant and the income tax worked out by Commission on the basis of ROE._ 41. Section 181 of the Electricity Act, 2003 grants State Commissions quasilegislative power to frame regulations consistent with the provision of the Act and accordingly Regulations framed under Section 181, like referred DERC regulations have the force of subordinate legislation. They bind the Commission itself, licensees, and stakeholders until struck down or modified by a competent judicial authority. The Supreme court in “ _**PTC India Ltd. v. CERC” (2010) 4 SCC 603**_ has held that regulations framed under Section 178 and181 are binding and have the force of law, however, they are subject to judicial review on the ground of being ultra vires the parent statute. **S** ection 111 of the Electricity act **c** onfers appellate jurisdiction upon this Tribunal over orders of State Commissions, however it does not have powers for judicial review of the Regulations framed under section 178 and 181 of the Electricity Act and thus cannot disregard the valid regulations while deciding the Appeals. It is also well settled that regulations, being subordinate legislation, must conform to the Electricity Act, 2003 and constitutional principles. If inconsistent, they can be struck down by constitutional courts. This Tribunal, while interpreting such regulations, may ensure conformity of orders with the Act and regulations, but it does not possess the jurisdiction to invalidate the regulations themselves.. We however find that in the Tribunal’s judgment dated 01.02.2016, no finding was made that Regulation 5.25 was inconsistent with the Electricity Act. Unless such inconsistency is judicially declared, the regulation continues to bind. _b. Judgment dated 02.12.2013 in Appeal No. 138 of 2012 in the case of Reliance Infrastructure Limited v. MERC;_ _222. Further, this Tribunal vide judgment dated 22.03.2024 in Appeal No. 283 of 2017 has considered the aforesaid appeals as under:_ _“68. The Respondents have contended that Regulation 22.3 provides that the RoE has to be grossed up with actual tax paid whereas the Appellant has contended that RoE is to be grossed up with the applicable tax payable._ _59. The issue is decided accordingly. The Commission is directed to reassess the Income tax liability of the Appellant as per our findings above and issue consequential orders._ _225. Hence the Commission is directed to compute and allow the Tax based on ROE. The issue, thus, is decided in favour of the Appellant “._ In view of the above deliberations, decision on all the issues is summarized in following table: The captioned appeal is partly allowed. The State Commission, is directed to pass consequential order on the issues remanded, as expeditiously as possible, preferably within a period of four months from the date of receipt of this judgement. Captioned Appeal, along with all pending IAs, if any, are disposed of in above terms.
title: DELHI TRANSCO LIMITED VERSUS DELHI ELECTRICITY REGULATORY COMMISSION & Ors
